children: This is the third in a special series on the challenge of building an architect-designed custom home for less than $1 million.

Charles Tesler, 64, has long known that he wanted to live full time in Amagansett, N.Y., where his family has had property since the 1960s. Twenty-five years ago, he bought an acre of land in Amagansett for $200,000. But for years, his job as a landscape architect for the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation's capital-projects division kept him in the city. And Amagansett, in the Hamptons, is one of the most expensive places to live in the U.S., with a median home sales price of $2.998 million, according to the data-research company PropertyShark.

Although he had no immediate plans to build a house, he went to work drawing up a design because he knew getting permits could be difficult and take time. He planned a 4,500-square-foot, four-bedroom stucco traditional, with lots of trim and a gabled roof, and started the process of getting permits.

In 2019, ready to make the move, Tesler wanted to reduce building costs. Plus, "I realized I didn't need that much space," he said. Research into alternative designs led him to a book called "Modern Modular" by architect Joseph Tanney.

Tesler took the house plans he'd drawn to Tanney, who reduced the planned home to a 2,250-square-foot, modern house. Tanney's crucial recommendation to keep costs down was that the house be built using modular-or prefabricated-construction. "That's the only way we could accomplish it," said Tanney.

The resulting three-bedroom, three-bathroom house was finished in December 2021. About 80% of the wood-frame house was built off-site, and the project ended up costing around $975,000, about 25% less than it would have cost to build it by hand on site, Tanney estimated.

Finding a builder willing to construct the house took 10 months, with bids coming in as high as $2 million. "People were uncomfortable with the modular process," Tesler said. Eventually he signed with Cruz Brothers Construction, which offered a fixed-cost contract, setting a price for the project up front.

By then, prices had started to increase on appliances and materials, so Tesler made reductions. He took out several windows, substituted three windows for a glass sliding door, and cut the walnut built-ins from a guest room and laundry room while keeping them in the living room.

Tesler's house was delivered by truck to his property in seven pieces: one each for the primary suite, kitchen, dining room, living room, TV room and a guest room, plus another that included the entry, laundry room, bathroom and an office.
Tesler, who bought all the appliances himself, was on the job site every day, supervising. He handled putting in the pool and landscaping himself.
He now lives in the completed house full time. Set amid the dunes near the beach, the lot has a scenic easement to the south and east, and reserved areas with wetlands to the north and south.
The finished house, a simple structure with courtyards and decks, is "like a city loft in the dunes," Tesler said.
The process showed him that "less is more," he said. "There's very little I'd change today if I did it again."
